edits.quote: Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7    [page number set flush right]
edits.fix: Use the standard footer with an id on every page, e.g. "Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7 / K1-1".

edits.quote: Problem 3: It is your turn. Circle the counters you take to be sure to win, or cross out the pile if you cannot be sure to win.
edits.fix: This repeats Problem 1's instruction word for word for piles 10, 11, 12. Fold these three piles into Problem 1 (piles 1-5 and 10-12 under one question), or put them right after piles 1-5, so the instruction is read once and the 1st/2nd question in Problem 2 does not split one task in two.

edits.quote: Diagram: 8 rows of 4 counters and 10 rows of 5 counters for 'every different way' a game of 4 and of 5 can go (there are 5 ways and 8 ways)
edits.fix: Kindergartners will try to fill every row and invent duplicates. Cut to about 6 rows of 4 and 9 rows of 5 so the spare rows are few, and consider moving this record-the-games problem up next to Problem 1, where listing every game of 4 and 5 feeds the trap work.

k-1.summary: A well-built K-1 sheet: concrete counter pictures, correct answers throughout (traps at multiples of 3, at multiples of 4 for {1,2,3}, at 1 mod 3 for last-loses, and the 1-and-4 two-pile surprise), and enough contrasting work for a full session. Only light edits are needed: a footer id, a repeated instruction in Problem 3, and too many spare rows in Problem 6.

edits.quote: Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7    [page number set flush right]
edits.fix: Use the standard footer with an id on every page, e.g. "Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7 / G23-1".

edits.quote: When the two piles are the same size, which player can always win? Explain why.  [diagram: pairs 3&3, 4&2, 4&1, 5&3]
edits.fix: Only one drawn pair (3 and 3) has equal piles, so the general question rests on a single example. Add one or two more equal pairs (e.g. 2&2, 5&5) and another unequal second-player pair (e.g. 5&2) so children have contrasting cases to play before generalizing.

grades-2-3.summary: Strong and correct: the claims to test (Lee right, Mo wrong; Jo right at 7, Kai wrong at 8) target the 'answer every reply' kernel, the {1,3,4} table extends to 30/50/61/100 (second, take 1, take 3, second), and the {1,3,5} parity task and the inverse 'multiples of 5' rule problem (any set containing 1-4 and no multiple of 5) give real challenge. The only edits are a footer id and too few equal-pile examples in Problem 7.

edits.quote: Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7    [page number set flush right]
edits.fix: Use the standard footer with an id on every page, e.g. "Bellingham Math Circle / Week 7 / G45-1".

edits.quote: When the two piles are the same size, which player can always win? Explain why.
edits.fix: The mirror argument for equal piles is the easy part and repeats the grades 2-3 question; the grid's real content is the off-diagonal second-player squares (1&4, 2&5, 0&3, 3&6, 1&7, ...). Replace with: "Describe all the squares you shaded and explain how the second player wins from each."

grades-4-5.summary: Mathematically rich and correct: {1,3,4} gives losing piles 0 and 2 mod 7 (100 losing, 1000 take 4, 2026 take 1 or 3), the four-game comparison contrasts {1,2} and {1,2,4} (same pattern) with {1,4} and {1,3,5}, greedy fails except in {1,3,5}, the multiples-of-4 problem has exactly four answers, last-loses shifts the pattern by one, and the {1,3,4} two-pile grid has five unequal second-player pairs. Only a footer id and a too-easy closing question in Problem 8 need changing.

overall.strongest: The grades 4-5 pages carry the outline's central idea (repeating win/lose patterns, why they repeat, and how they change with the rule) through a well-chosen, fully correct sequence with clean grids and no decorative text.
overall.weakest: The K-1 pages are the least tidy: Problem 3 repeats Problem 1's instruction and Problem 6 has too many spare rows for kindergartners, though both take only minutes to fix.
